abstract: >-
  Most EEG source imaging methods assume brain activity arises from independent, focal sources and are validated mainly on their ability to localize a single generator — overlooking the brain's network structure and the propagation of activity along it. We introduce weighted Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (wCSET), which replaces its predecessor CSET's L1 sparsity prior with a smooth, exponentially weighted L2 prior over the connectome-harmonic spectrum. We validate wCSET, CSET, three standard connectivity-agnostic methods, and a geometry-based (Laplace-Beltrami) alternative across three complementary studies that probe source reconstruction beyond localization: simulated activity propagating across a structural connectome, providing an exact network-level ground truth; a clinical cohort of 26 seizure-free epilepsy patients, using the resected epileptogenic zone as ground truth; and simultaneous scalp and intracranial EEG recordings, a rare direct electrophysiological benchmark. In simulation, wCSET matched standard methods at localizing a source's onset but substantially outperformed them at reconstructing its subsequent propagation, an advantage robust to noise and to considerable connectome corruption. In the resection cohort, wCSET preserved localization accuracy while requiring markedly less reconstructed cortex to reach the true epileptogenic zone than any competitor. Against intracranial recordings, wCSET outperformed standard and connectivity-agnostic methods in one of two evaluable subjects, but was itself outperformed by a purely geometric alternative in both — suggesting cortical geometry alone may capture much of what drives accurate distributed reconstruction. Together, these results establish wCSET as a principled step beyond localization-only source imaging, and introduce a validation framework for evaluating such methods against a source's full activity pattern rather than its location alone.

# Introduction

Electroencephalography (EEG) offers unparalleled temporal resolution for studying neural dynamics _in vivo_ — but scalp recordings pay for it in spatial resolution [@nunez_electric_2006]. Source reconstruction was devised to recover some of that lost precision: project the EEG signal onto a cortical surface modeled from the individual's own MRI, marrying EEG's timing with structural imaging's geometry. The Minimum Norm Estimate (MNE), introduced in 1993, was the first such method [@dale_improved_1993].

Three decades of variants followed — sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002], eLORETA [@pascual-marqui_discrete_2007], dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000], LCMV [@van_veen_localization_1997] — but the goal barely changed: pinpoint the isolated region behind a signal, a practice known as source localization [@knosche_eegmeg_2022]. Neuroscience, meanwhile, has moved on. Connectivity approaches now treat the brain as an integrated network rather than a set of independent regions [@bressler_large-scale_2010], and localization-focused methods are increasingly out of step with that view.

The mismatch runs deeper than terminology. These methods assume independent sources, a prior known to underperform one informed by the true source covariance [@wipf_unified_2009] — defensible when activity is genuinely focal, but not once multiple regions are involved. Because the EEG inverse problem is ill-posed, reconstructed activity from interacting sources then blurs together across the cortex, a phenomenon known as leakage or field spread [@schoffelen_source_2009; @gonzalez-moreira_caulking_2018]. No prior can undo that ill-posedness, but a structured one can at least contain its damage [@gonzalez-moreira_caulking_2018].

Several strategies try to close that gap. Functional priors from fMRI can constrain expected interactions [@liu_fmri-si-stbf_2021], though fMRI's hemodynamic response unfolds over seconds — too slow to meaningfully constrain millisecond-scale EEG dynamics. Agnostic approaches instead jointly estimate source activity and its covariance structure from the data itself, at the cost of greater ill-posedness and computation (e.g., BC-VARETA [@gonzalez-moreira_third_2018]). A third strategy leans on structure–function coupling directly: since neural activity propagates along the brain's structural scaffolding, the connectome estimated from diffusion MRI tractography offers a principled, subject-specific prior instead [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024].

Graph Signal Processing (GSP) supplies the machinery for this coupling [@shuman_emerging_2013]. Eigendecomposing the connectome's graph Laplacian yields brain harmonics ordered by graph frequency: low frequencies capture smooth, globally integrated activity, high frequencies more locally segregated patterns [@shuman_emerging_2013; @atasoy_human_2016]. Projecting source activity onto this basis — the Graph Fourier Transform (Section 2.3.3) — yields a compact "connectome spectrum," since both fMRI and EEG source activity concentrate their energy in a handful of low-frequency harmonics [@rue-queralt_connectome_2021; @atasoy_human_2016]. Rué-Queralt et al. (2024) built on this: Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (CSET) enforces an L₁ sparsity prior in this spectrum, restricting solutions to a small number of active harmonics.

A parallel line of work asks whether geometry alone can do the job. Substituting the Beltrami-Laplace operator on the cortical mesh for the connectome's graph Laplacian trades long-range white-matter pathways for fine-grained local geometry [@pang_geometric_2023] — and works about as well: Pang et al. (2023) found the resulting geometric eigenmodes reconstruct functional activity at least as accurately as connectome-based ones. Wang et al. (2026) pushed this further with Geometric Basis Functions (GBF): whole-brain activity as a combination of the leading ~200 such eigenmodes under a logarithmically-decaying L₂ penalty [@wang_geometry_2026]. Siu et al. took a different route to the same idea, using weighted Beltrami harmonics as a hard post-hoc spectral filter rather than a continuous penalty [@siu_structural_2026].

CSET, however, has no principled way to tell biologically meaningful harmonics from noise-dominated ones — unlike the geometry-based methods above, which weight low-order harmonics preferentially by construction. We close that gap with weighted CSET (wCSET): a weighted L₂ prior that decays exponentially with graph frequency, replacing CSET's L₁ prior with a continuous, eigenvalue-graded penalty in GBF's spirit, but applied to the connectome's graph Laplacian, retaining the white-matter awareness the geometry-based methods lack. The weighting is not arbitrary: Abdelnour et al. (2018) show that functional connectivity's eigenvalues relate to the structural Laplacian's via an approximately exponential mapping, so a small number of low-frequency structural eigenmodes already dominate functional connectivity [@abdelnour_functional_2018].

Despite this progression toward increasingly principled spectral weightings, validation has not kept pace. Rué-Queralt et al. validated CSET by correlating reconstructed activity with fMRI from the same task — but fMRI's hemodynamic response reflects neural activity only indirectly and with substantial temporal blurring, making it a weak proxy for the electrophysiological ground truth these methods aim to reconstruct. Other works validate through source localization in epilepsy patients instead; even where source extent improves, the criterion is misaligned with what connectivity-informed methods are designed to capture — not a focal source's spatial footprint, but the dynamics of activity across interconnected networks, a capability localization accuracy does not measure.

The primary barrier to a more appropriate validation is simpler than it sounds: no ground truth exists for interconnected neural dynamics. We build one, on three complementary fronts. First, we simulate activity propagating across the structural connectome itself (Section 2.1.1), giving an exact, fully known ground truth for network-level dynamics that no empirical recording can offer. Second, in a clinical cohort where the resected epileptogenic zone serves as ground truth, we introduce the Network Concentration Index (Section 2.6.3), which asks how tightly reconstructed activity concentrates onto the resection as a whole, not just its single most active vertex. Third, we revive and extend Grova et al. (2016)'s framework [@grova_intracranial_2016] correlating MEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG), extending it to truly simultaneous EEG/iEEG recordings — the only electrophysiological ground truth free from neurovascular coupling, skull attenuation, and temporal blurring [@nunez_electric_2006] — obtained by projecting EEG-reconstructed sources onto iEEG electrode locations for direct comparison.

Building on this three-part framework, we evaluate CSET and wCSET across three complementary studies:

- **Study I:** Using simulations of spontaneous source diffusion via dMRI-based structural connectivity, we show that while standard methods accurately localize a source's _onset_, connectivity-informed methods are significantly superior at capturing its _propagation_, and we assess robustness to erroneous connectivity data.

- **Study II:** Using a clinical epilepsy dataset where post-surgical success defines ground truth, the Network Concentration Index shows connectivity-informed methods concentrate reconstructed activity more tightly onto the resected zone than standard methods, without sacrificing localization accuracy.

- **Study III:** Using simultaneous EEG/iEEG recordings, we validate source reconstruction directly against intracranial measurements, demonstrating connectivity-informed methods' ability to map dynamic neural networks beyond point-source localization.

Together, these studies establish wCSET as a principled, viable tool for reconstructing distributed brain dynamics, and introduce a multi-level validation framework that moves the field beyond localization as the benchmark for source imaging.


# Materials and Methods

## Data Acquisition and Datasets

### Synthetic Data

Simulations used anatomical data from a single representative VEPCON subject [@pascucci_source_2022] (T1-weighted MRI and DTI tractogram), with EEG simulated on the 204-channel montage used throughout (Section 2.1.2). The cortical source space (Section 2.3.1) was parcellated into ~400 regions via the MultiConn atlas [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022], from which 100 were selected by farthest-point sampling as a spatially uniform probe set — reused throughout except for the noise-robustness analysis (Section 3.1.2), which instead uses a separate, independently-sampled 50-region subset (rationale in Annex).

In each trial, a source region drawn from the probe set was assigned a 50 ms double-Hanning-window spike waveform (mimicking a clinical interictal spike) on all its dipoles, following approaches modelling epileptiform activity as a patch of simultaneously active dipoles rather than a point source [@afnan_eegmeg_2024] (waveform definition in Annex). The spike repeated every 1 s across a 20 s recording; after propagation and sensor projection (below and Section 2.2), the 20 resulting events were epoched and averaged into a single evoked response per run.

**Propagation model.** Activity was propagated across the connectome in a feedforward manner, with each dipole's activity a delayed and spatially-decayed copy of the source waveform:

$$
S_j(t) = \gamma^{h_j} \cdot s_0\!\left(t - \tau_j\right)
$$

where $h_j$ is the hop count from source to dipole $j$, $\gamma = 0.5$ is a per-hop spatial decay factor, and $\tau_j$ is a propagation delay based on conduction speed, nodal delay, and timing jitter (full model in Annex).

**Noise model.** Pink noise (source level) and white noise (sensor level) were calibrated to a literature-typical 15 µV RMS baseline [@nunez_electric_2006] and a single-trial SNR of 5 (@tbl-sim-params; full derivation in Annex).

Each simulation was repeated 8 times per source region; region/repetition counts were set via a power analysis for the region-paired comparisons reported in Results (full analysis in Annex).

### Clinical Dataset A — Resection Cohort

We used the dataset of @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025 to validate EEG source imaging clinically: 44 patients with pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy who underwent resective surgery, outcome graded on the ILAE scale at 12 months (1 = seizure-free, 2–6 = increasing persistent seizures). We restricted analysis to seizure-free outcomes (ILAE 1, 28 patients) — for residual-seizure patients, the resection may not fully encompass the true epileptogenic zone, an unreliable ground truth — and excluded two more (no genuine resection cavity; missing EEG channel locations for coregistration), leaving 26 patients. Each had a pre- and post-operative T1-weighted MRI and a pre-operative interictal EEG recording (resection masks per Section 2.5.1); discharges had been visually identified by clinical experts among the dataset's authors and time-locked averaged at their peak. The dataset's 257-channel EEG (HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net) was reduced to the 204-channel montage used throughout by excluding cheek electrodes. As individual diffusion MRI was unavailable, the structural connectome was instead derived from the population probabilistic tractography atlas (Section 2.3.3).


### Clinical Dataset B — Simultaneous EEG/iEEG Cohort

To validate source reconstruction against ground-truth intracranial activity, we used a cohort of 4 patients (sub-12, sub-34, sub-48, sub-50) with simultaneously recorded scalp EEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG) (recruitment, implantation, and ethics details in Annex — **TODO: to be filled in by the co-author**).

Interictal discharges were identified and epoched in both modalities, time-locked to the same events, yielding paired scalp/intracranial recordings of the same underlying activity. Each patient's pre-operative T1-weighted MRI was processed identically to the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A) for anatomical/forward modeling (Section 2.3), and the structural connectome was derived the same way (individual diffusion MRI was likewise unavailable). Results are reported in the main text for the two subjects with a visible scalp EEG spike; the other two had deep sources with no visible spike, making their EEG-derived reconstruction — and the virtual iEEG projected from it (Section 2.5.2) — inherently unreliable, so their results appear in the supplementary material instead.

## Signal Preprocessing

### EEG/iEEG Processing

**Studies 1 and 3.** EEG was epoched time-locked to the interictal spike peak (the simulated source's peak in Study 1; the simultaneous iEEG signal's peak in Study 3, not one independently detected on the scalp), with a Common Average Reference [@bertrand_theoretical_1985], baseline correction, and noise-covariance estimation from the pre-spike period. Epochs were averaged into the evoked response: 20 per run in Study 1, 130–265 marked spikes per subject in Study 3. Study 3's channel comparison (Section 2.6.4) instead used an adaptive GFP-threshold window rather than @grova_intracranial_2016's fixed-sample one (criterion in Annex).

**Study 2.** EEG arrived as pre-averaged discharges, already filtered, downsampled, and interpolated by the data providers (@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025; parameters in Annex); without individual epochs, noise-covariance estimation and whitening were skipped. A Common Average Reference, a notch filter for residual 50 Hz noise, and baseline correction were applied where needed.

**iEEG.** Intracranial recordings were epoched time-locked to the spike peak and averaged directly into the ground-truth evoked response, with no further preprocessing.

## Forward Modeling and Structural Priors

### Source Space

Neural activity was modeled using a distributed dipole model with a cortical constraint: the source space restricted to the cortical white matter surface, reconstructed from T1-weighted MRI using FreeSurfer, with ~7,600 dipoles uniformly distributed across it via MNE-Python [@gramfort_meg_2013] at ~3.3 mm average spacing, orientations fixed normal to the cortical manifold (full subdivision scheme, tool versions, and orientation-constraint rationale in Annex).

### Volume Conduction Model

Volume conduction was modeled with a Boundary Element Model (BEM) [@hamalainen_realistic_1989] using MNE-Python's default conductivities (0.3 S/m brain/scalp, 0.006 S/m skull). Because MNE-Python's default FreeSurfer watershed extraction often yields sub-optimal BEM geometries, we instead built the head model with a custom SimNIBS CHARM-based pipeline [@puonti_accurate_2020], fitting inner skull, outer skull, and scalp surfaces sequentially and non-intersecting (full pipeline in Annex; BEM comparison in supplementary) <!-- supp fig (BEM models)-->. EEG sensors were pre-co-registered to the T1-weighted MRI and thus intrinsically aligned with the head model; the resulting forward solution (gain matrix), computed via MNE-Python, was used across all three studies.

For Study 1 only, a second forward solution used a deliberately mismatched skull conductivity (0.012 S/m, brain/scalp unchanged) to avoid the inverse crime [@wirgin_inverse_2004] — the circularity of using the same head model to both generate and invert simulated data, which inflates apparent accuracy (precedent in Annex); the two models differ by ~10% (supplementary) <!-- supp fig (Head model differences)-->.

### Connectivity Matrices

The brain is modeled as a graph (connectome) whose nodes are the source-space dipoles and whose edges — used by CSET and its weighted version wCSET — represent physical anatomical links between them.

**Empirical connectomes**

Two types of structural links are incorporated: long-range connections from dMRI tractography, and short-range connections linking each dipole to its geodesically nearest neighbors, capturing local gray matter connectivity missed by standard tractography (thresholds in Annex); edges are weighted by distance — fiber length for long-range, geodesic distance for local.

**Connectome surrogates**

Where diffusion data is unavailable clinically, we evaluate three connectome surrogates, validated via our simulation framework (Section 3.1) and summarized in @tbl-surrogates; two are also tested binarized (edge presence only) to isolate topology from edge-weight fidelity — five variants total.

| Local | Gray matter connectivity only, plus homotopic cross-hemisphere links to keep the graph connected (Annex) | Yes | Local geometry alone, without long-range information, suffices |

**Connectome perturbation**

To test robustness to imperfect connectome knowledge, we perturb the connectome before source reconstruction (Section 3.1.2) via a degree-preserving double-edge swap (two random edges re-paired, degree unchanged), at severities from 0–100% of total edges.

**Graph Fourier Transform**
For the Laplacian, edge weights are inverted — closer, more direct connections thus carrying proportionally more weight — to populate the adjacency matrix A, from which the graph Laplacian L = D − A (D the degree matrix) enables Graph Signal Processing (GSP) on neural data [@shuman_emerging_2013; @ortega_graph_2018]. The Graph Fourier Transform (GFT) decomposes brain activity into graph harmonics — the eigenvectors $u_k$ of L — via the eigendecomposition:
$$
\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top
$$

where $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ contains the eigenvalues (graph frequencies) and $\mathbf{U} = [u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_N]$ forms the orthonormal eigenbasis.


## Source Reconstruction Framework

Every study used MNE-Python's wMNE [@dale_improved_1993], dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000], and sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002] (full derivation in Annex) as standard baselines against three connectivity-informed methods: CSET, wCSET, and GBF (Section 2.4.1). All methods whitened using an empirically estimated noise covariance [@dale_dynamic_2000; @knosche_eegmeg_2022], except the resection cohort, whose pre-averaged discharges had no baseline epochs to estimate one from — an ad-hoc identity covariance was used instead (no whitening).

In the M/EEG inverse problem, we aim to estimate underlying dipole activities $\mathbf s\in \mathbb R^n$ from observed sensor measurements $\mathbf y \in \mathbb R^m$ via the forward model $\mathbf y = \mathbf L \mathbf s + \epsilon$, where $\mathbf L$ is the lead-field matrix; because $n\gg m$, the problem is ill-posed. Assuming a Gaussian source prior turns reconstruction into a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate — the regularized least-squares problem:

$$
\mathbf s^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\underbrace{\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf s\rVert_2^2}_{\text{Data Fidelity}} + \lambda\underbrace{\lVert \mathbf C \mathbf s\rVert_p^p}_{\text{Regularization}} \tag{1}
$$

where $\lambda$ balances data fit against the prior, and $\mathbf C^T\mathbf C = \mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s}^{-1}$ is derived from the (generally unknown) source covariance $\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$. wMNE, dSPM and sLORETA all replace $\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$ with the identity matrix — the assumption of independent, equal-variance sources that gives these methods their "independent-source" label throughout this work — with wMNE additionally applying a depth-weighting matrix $\mathbf W_d$ (exponent $\kappa=0.8$; full formula in Annex) to counteract the bias of $l_2$-regularized solutions toward superficial dipoles; CSET and wCSET reuse this same matrix below, with a different exponent (full Bayesian derivation, parameter justification, and sLORETA/dSPM's post-hoc standardization in Annex).

### Connectivity-Informed Inverse Solution

Three connectivity-informed inverse solutions are compared: CSET, wCSET (this work's central contribution), and GBF.

**Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography**

CSET [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024] projects source activity onto the connectome's eigenmodes ($\mathbf U$) — the connectome spectrum — and, like wMNE, counteracts superficial-dipole bias with the same depth-weighting matrix $\mathbf W_d$, but with $\kappa=0.2$ rather than wMNE's $\kappa=0.8$, tuned against reconstruction accuracy in simulation (Section 3.1).

Since the connectome spectrum is compact, CSET enforces sparsity via an $l_1$-norm regularizer. Let $\mathbf {\hat s}$ represent the spectrum of $\mathbf s$ (where $\mathbf s = \mathbf W_d\mathbf U \mathbf {\hat s}$). Equation (1) is then modified to:
$$
\mathbf {\hat s}^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf W_d\mathbf U \mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_1 \tag{2}
$$

The physical brain activity is then recovered via $\mathbf s^* = \mathbf W_d\mathbf U\mathbf{\hat s}^*$.

**weighted CSET**

Weighted CSET (wCSET) replaces CSET's $l_1$ sparsity prior with a smooth, weighted $l_2$ prior. Harmonic weights follow an exponential low-pass filter on graph frequency, $W_{h,ii} = \exp(-\beta\lambda_i)$ ($\lambda_i$: harmonic $i$'s eigenvalue; $\beta$: decay rate, tuned against reconstruction accuracy; motivation in the Introduction). Equation (2) thus becomes:

$$
\mathbf {\hat s}^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf W_d\mathbf U \mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf W_h\mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_2^2 \tag{3}
$$

where $\mathbf W_h$ is the diagonal matrix of harmonic weights above. The physical brain activity is again recovered via $\mathbf s^* = \mathbf W_d\mathbf U\mathbf{\hat s}^*$.

**Geometric Basis Functions**

As a further reference method, wCSET (Eq. 3) is reconfigured to approximate Wang et al. (2026)'s Geometric Basis Functions (GBF) [@wang_geometry_2026]: the cortical mesh's Laplace-Beltrami eigenbasis (Section 2.3.3) instead of the connectome's, no depth weighting, and GBF's hard-truncated, log-form weighting with cutoff $S=150$ instead of the exponential one (formula and $S$ tuning in Annex; not GBF's exact pipeline). This geometry-only comparator (in the spirit of [@pang_geometric_2023; @wang_geometry_2026; @siu_structural_2026], Section 1) is tested as a connectome surrogate (Section 3.1.4) and as a full fourth method in both clinical studies (Sections 3.2, 3.3).

## Clinical Ground Truth Definition

Ground-truth brain activity maps aren't directly available clinically, so we rely on proxies: for the resection cohort (Section 2.1.2), the resected area (segmented per Section 2.5.1), since these symptom-free-after-surgery patients' resections mark the epileptogenic zone; for the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort (Section 2.1.3), intracranial recordings, which give ground-truth potential only at sparse electrode locations, so reconstructed dipole-current maps are instead projected onto them via a simplified forward model (Section 2.5.2) for direct comparison.

### Resected Area Segmentation

For the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A), resection masks were generated with RAMPS [@simpson_automated_2025], estimating resected volume from pre-/post-operative T1-weighted MRI plus the resection's hemisphere and lobe (clinical record or visual comparison; Annex), then visually QC'd (overlaying pre-/post-operative T1w and mask), with manual segmentation replacing unusable automated masks; subjects whose mask remained missing, incomplete, or incorrect were excluded (Section 2.1.2).

### Source-to-iEEG Projection

For the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort (Clinical Dataset B), reconstructed cortical activity was projected onto the intracranial electrode coordinates as "virtual" iEEG, following Grova et al. (2016) [@grova_intracranial_2016]: an infinite homogeneous conduction model with tissue conductivity set to 0.25 S/m (vs. the standard 0.33 S/m) per Cosandier-Rimélé et al. (2007) [@cosandier-rimele_physiologically_2007] to compensate for the model's simplifications. Assuming 3 mm iEEG-MRI coregistration accuracy, the potential $\Phi$ at $r$ is stabilized against near-source instability with the same adjustment:

$$
\begin{align}\Phi(r) &= \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_i)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3} \text{ if } r>r_0 = 3 \text{ mm} \\ \Phi(r) &= \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3} \text{ if } r\le r_0 = 3 \text{ mm}\end{align}
$$

## Performance Evaluation Metrics

### Map to map comparison

Each method is evaluated via the (signed) Pearson spatial correlation between reconstructed and ground-truth activity maps at each time point:
$$
\mathcal{C}(t) = \frac{\sum_i \mathbf{s}^t_{\text{true}}(i) \cdot \mathbf{s}^t_{\text{est}}(i)}{\sigma_{\text{true}}(t) \cdot \sigma_{\text{est}}(t)}
$$

where $\mathbf s^t_{x}(i)$ is the activity at dipole $i$ and time $t$, and $\sigma_{x}(t)$ is the standard deviation of map $x$ at time $t$.

### Localization Accuracy

Source onset was defined relative to the discharge's rising phase, balancing a low probability of already-started propagation (favoring onset) against adequate SNR (favoring the peak, by which the source has typically spread). For both cohorts we used 25% of the rising phase (quarter rising phase, qrp), earlier than @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020's 50% convention, and computed the Euclidean distance from the location of maximal source activity to the target mask boundary (the true seed region for simulation, the resection volume for the resection cohort) — following @carboni_linear_2022 and @wang_geometry_2026 rather than averaging over several nearest voxels, with distance 0 mm if that location already lies inside the mask. For the resection cohort, this was additionally computed at the peak, to test whether accuracy holds once the source has spread (Section 3.2).

### Network Concentration Index

Peak-vertex localization accuracy only tests whether the single most active location falls near the resection; since interictal discharges may arise from a distributed set of regions only partially captured by the resected tissue [@spencer_neural_2002; @kramer_epilepsy_2012], we complement it with the Network Concentration Index (NCI), a cluster-extent thresholding procedure [@friston_assessing_1994]. Cortical vertices are ranked by activity and progressively marked active from the highest down; at each step, active vertices are grouped into contiguous clusters, and any cluster smaller than 600 mm² — the minimum synchronously active cortex needed for a scalp-visible discharge [@grova_evaluation_2006] — is discarded, continuing until one surviving cluster first touches the resection (full procedure in Annex). NCI is the percentage of cortex marked active at that point; lower values mean a smaller, more concentrated portion of the network sufficed to reach the resection. It is computed at the quarter rising phase and peak, and calibrated against a chance level — the percentage a purely random activity map needs before any cluster reaches the 600 mm² floor, regardless of resection overlap (procedure in Annex).

### Channel comparison

The projected virtual iEEG activity (Section 2.5.2) was compared against ground-truth iEEG via polarity-invariant Pearson correlation ($|r|$, since sign flips are an arbitrary artifact of the virtual-electrode reference, not a real failure), computed spatially (across channels, per timepoint) and temporally (across time, per channel), plus a win-rate for each competitor against wCSET — the fraction of channels/timepoints where wCSET is closer to ground truth — rather than a full all-against-all comparison.

### Statistical Analysis

Method comparisons are paired (by region for simulation, by subject for the resection cohort, by channel/timepoint for Study 3) and tested against a reference method, typically wCSET. Discrete outcomes (localization error, NCI) used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (rank-biserial effect size); where the matched dimension carries serial or spatial correlation — Study 3's channel comparison (Section 2.6.4) — we instead used a paired t-test with an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size (Cohen's dz; full derivation in Annex). Continuous comparisons along a coordinate (SNR, time, perturbation severity) used cluster-based permutation testing (full procedure in Annex), with all p-values Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-corrected within their comparison family at α = 0.05.
# Results

# Formatting helpers for inline-quoted statistics throughout the Results and
# Discussion sections below - defined once here so every `{python} ...`
# inline reference downstream uses the same rounding/threshold convention,
# rather than re-implementing it at each of the many call sites. Numbers
# quoted in prose are pulled live from the same `stat.wilcoxon`/`.ttest_ess`/
# `.cluster_permutation` calls that build the figures (computed and
# cached once by each processing_*.qmd's Statistics section, reloaded here
# as an instant cache hit), rather than hand-typed, so that changing a test
# and re-rendering updates the prose automatically instead of silently
# drifting from what the code produces.
def fmt_p(p, thresh=0.001):
    """Bare comparison + value for prose, e.g. '< 0.001' or '= 0.023' - the
    prose supplies its own 'p'/'p_corrected' label immediately before the
    inline reference (e.g. `` p`{python} fmt_p(...)` `` renders 'p = 0.023'
    or 'p < 0.001'), since which label applies varies by context."""
    return f"< {thresh}" if p < thresh else f"= {p:.3f}"

# Reference-method annotation for the group_comparison/cluster_permutation
# figures below - neither mindmap function exposes a hook to customize its
# legend/tick-label text, so these mutate what's already drawn (in place, not
# replacing it) rather than reaching into the mindmap package itself.
def mark_reference(ax, reference, suffix=" (ref.)"):
    """Appends `suffix` to `reference`'s entry in `ax`'s already-built legend, in place."""
    for text in ax.get_legend().get_texts():
        if text.get_text() == reference:
            text.set_text(text.get_text() + suffix)
            break

def ref_labels(names, reference, suffix=" (ref.)"):
    """Tick-label list with `suffix` appended to `reference`'s entry."""
    return [f"{n}{suffix}" if n == reference else n for n in names]

def fmt_stat(value, digits=2):
    """Effect size (rank-biserial, Cohen's dz, etc.) for prose, e.g. '-0.48'."""
    return f"{value:.{digits}f}"

def fmt_num(value, digits=1):
    """Plain descriptive number (medians, mm, %, correlation units) for prose."""
    return f"{value:.{digits}f}"

def main_cluster(cluster_df):
    """The largest-mass cluster from a single competitor's
    `ClusterResult.clusters_by_pair[(reference, competitor)]` table -
    the one worth quoting in prose when a competitor has more than one
    (typically one real cluster plus a few negligible-mass leftovers)."""
    return cluster_df.loc[cluster_df["mass"].abs().idxmax()]

def competitor_row(result, competitor, reference="wcset"):
    """Row for one competitor from a `PairwiseResult.table` - the new API's
    table has arbitrary `group_a`/`group_b` columns instead of the old
    `"Label"` column, so this looks up whichever side of the pair
    `competitor` landed on."""
    t = result.table
    row = t[(t["group_a"] == reference) & (t["group_b"] == competitor)]
    if row.empty:
        row = t[(t["group_a"] == competitor) & (t["group_b"] == reference)]
    return row.iloc[0]

### Robustness to Data Noise

Sweeping simulated target SNR from 20 down to 1 (Section 2.1.1), localization error rose for every method as SNR decreased, but wMNE alone accounted for most of that degradation — the other four methods stayed low until roughly SNR=4–5 before climbing (@fig-noise-localization). wCSET's spatial-correlation advantage over every competitor, found above at fixed noise (Section 3.1.1), held across nearly the full SNR range tested, down to SNR=1 (@fig-noise-correlation).

### Robustness to Prior Noise

Using the connectome-perturbation procedure of Section 2.3.3, we re-evaluated localization error and spatial correlation for CSET and wCSET, benchmarked against connectome-agnostic sLORETA (@fig-degradation-localization, @fig-degradation-correlation). Both methods started with a significant advantage over sLORETA at low-to-moderate degradation, but this reversed into a significant deficit for CSET at higher degradation levels; wCSET's advantage, by contrast, never reversed into a significant deficit, even under full (100%) connectome permutation.

### Spatial and Temporal Correlation Analysis

Source localization was inconclusive for connectivity-informed methods in Study II (Section 3.2.1). Since these methods are designed to capture distributed activity rather than a single focal source, we instead tested whether they better reproduce the overall pattern of activity, as Study I suggests they should.

Of the four subjects with usable simultaneous EEG/iEEG data (Section 2.1.3), two show a visible interictal spike on the scalp EEG; the other two have deep sources with no visible spike despite clear intracranial evidence of the same discharge, and are reported in the supplementary material. For each, wCSET was compared against every competitor at the channel level (temporal correlation) and timepoint level (spatial correlation), via the autocorrelation-corrected paired test of Section 2.6.5.

# is added to COMPETITORS below in processing_intra.qmd's own method order
# (["wcset", "sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne", "beltrami"]) rather than
# appended after METHODS's order, so this cell's stat.ttest_ess() calls stay
# an exact, byte-identical match to the ones already cached by that file's
# Statistics section.

# combined suite (every sub-*/ subfolder concatenated) built and stats-cached
# by processing_intra.qmd's Statistics section - loaded here directly, never
# combined via concat() in this document.
vieeg_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/intra/combined")

# Only 4 subjects total (fixed), and 2 of them (12, 50) have deep sources with
# no visible spike on scalp EEG -- their EEG-derived source reconstruction
# (and therefore virtual iEEG) starts from an inherently less reliable signal
# than 34/48's. Stats are still computed for all 4 (SUBJECT_ORDER) - reused
# by the supplementary material - but the main-text figure below only plots
# MAIN_SUBJECTS (34/48); 12/50 are reported in the supplementary material
# instead (see prose above).
SUBJECT_ORDER = ["34", "48", "12", "50"]
MAIN_SUBJECTS = ["48", "34"]
SUBJECT_TITLES = {
    "34": "Subject 2",
    "48": "Subject 1",
    "12": "sub-12\n(no visible EEG spike)",
    "50": "sub-50\n(no visible EEG spike)",
}

# Only 4 subjects - too few for subject-level pairing (pairing_col="Subject"
# would treat n=4 as the sample size, no real power). Channels/timepoints
# within one subject are numerous but NOT independent (spatially/temporally
# correlated), so a plain Wilcoxon/t-test paired across them would overstate
# significance. Fix: an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size
# (Thiebaux & Zwiers, 1984) in place of the raw channel/timepoint count -
# mindmap.core.stats.effective_sample_size, via
# suite.stat.ttest_ess(...) - see
# mindmap/tutorials/analysis/metrics/metricsuite-intra-vieeg.ipynb, which
# this cell adapts directly (measured lag-1 autocorrelation of the
# wCSET-competitor difference series on this exact data: 0.45-0.83 for
# timepoints, 0.16-0.52 for channels - large enough that the correction has
# real bite, not just a formality).
COMPETITORS = ["sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne", "beltrami"]


def paired_diffs(subject, metric, coord):
    # exact post-dropna order already computed and cached by
    # processing_intra.qmd's Statistics section - reused verbatim both to
    # rebuild this diffs array and to keep the stat.ttest_ess() call
    # below (part of the cache key) an instant cache hit rather than a
    # silent recompute under a different order.
    order = vieeg_metrics.metadata["derived"]["subject_order"][subject][metric]
    df_sub = vieeg_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"Subject": subject})
    wide = df_sub.pivot_table(index=coord, columns="Method", values="Value", aggfunc="mean").reindex(order)
    wide = wide.dropna(subset=["wcset"] + COMPETITORS)
    return {c: (wide["wcset"] - wide[c]).to_numpy() for c in COMPETITORS}, wide.index.tolist()


METRIC_BLOCKS = [
    ("correlation_temporal", "channel", "Temporal corr.\n(diff per channel)"),
    ("correlation_spatial", "times", "Spatial corr.\n(diff per timepoint)"),
]

# statistics quoted in the prose below and drawn by the figure at the end of
# this section are collected into these two dicts, keyed by (subject,
# metric) - so the figure and the prose numbers come from exactly the same
# stat.ttest_ess() call, run once here.
vieeg_results = {}
vieeg_diffs = {}

for metric, coord, ylabel in METRIC_BLOCKS:

        # identical call to the one already cached by processing_intra.qmd's
        # Statistics section.
        vieeg_results[(subject, metric)] = vieeg_metrics.stat.ttest_ess(
            metric, group_by="Method", comparisons=vieeg_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], COMPETITORS),
            pairing_col=coord, subject_order=order, filters={"Subject": subject},

def _winrate(subject, metric, competitor):
    return vieeg_metrics.metadata["derived"]["win_rate"][f"{subject}|{metric}|{competitor}"]

def _dz(subject, metric, competitor):
    # ttest_ess's own effect size (Cohen's dz on the wcset-competitor
    # difference series) - positive means wCSET wins, matching the
    # win-rate/diff sign convention used elsewhere in this cell.
    return competitor_row(vieeg_results[(subject, metric)], competitor)["effect_size"]

# Discussion

## Simulation Insights

Our connectome-driven propagation model lets a focal source recruit distant regions directly through long-range tracts rather than only spreading through neighbors step by step — a mechanism unavailable to nearest-neighbor spread, and impractical to reproduce with neural mass models at realistic dipole counts [@sanz-leon_mathematical_2015; @nunez_multi-scale_2019] (design rationale in Annex). Because the scalp signal sums every active dipole while the source's own amplitude decays with distance from the origin, the EEG peak systematically lags true onset — consistent with the clinical literature on interictal discharge propagation [@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020; @carboni_linear_2022], and the reason the field favors an earlier point in the rising phase for localization over the peak.

At that early, focal quarter-rising-phase point, wCSET localized about as accurately as CSET and dSPM and clearly outperformed wMNE, with a more modest advantage over sLORETA; with 100 regions behind each comparison, effect sizes rather than p-values separate these meaningful and negligible gaps. This is expected: connectivity information should help least while a source is still genuinely focal. Its role becomes clear once the source spreads: spatial correlation with ground truth improves for every method toward the peak, but far more for wCSET and CSET, consistent with the connectome-spectrum representation becoming more compact as activity spreads across the cortex [@rue-queralt_connectome_2021]. This advantage held broadly across single-trial SNR, and, under connectome degradation, wCSET's edge over sLORETA never reversed even under full (100%) edge permutation, unlike CSET's, which reversed into a deficit beyond 80% — a reassuring margin given how much false-positive structure real tractography can contain [@maier-hein_challenge_2017]. This robustness also guided wCSET's own design: an initial attempt to weight harmonics by robustness to perturbation itself [@sipes_integrative_2024] favored both very low- and very high-frequency harmonics, but the latter introduced reconstruction artifacts, leaving the smooth, low-frequency-favoring exponential decay that became wCSET.

That tolerance extended to a more radical test: substituting the true connectome for cheap, dMRI-free surrogates — an atlas prior, a local-geometry rule, or Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes — left wCSET's accuracy unchanged or slightly improved, with binarized and weighted variants performing almost identically, indicating the benefit rests on topology rather than precise edge weights. The Beltrami surrogate stood out, matching or marginally exceeding the true connectome despite the simulation being built directly around it — motivating why we carry a full Beltrami-based (GBF) variant into both clinical studies below.

## Epilepsy with Resected Ground Truth

The resection cohort echoed the simulation's localization picture: peak-to-resection distance did not differ significantly between wCSET, CSET, sLORETA, dSPM, or Beltrami, with wMNE again the outlier. Localization error was considerably worse here than in simulation, however, and reconstructions broke into several discrete, only partly overlapping clusters — reflecting either underestimated physiological noise in the simulation, or genuine multi-focal spread by the point clinical discharges are typically marked. This motivated the Network Concentration Index, which asks how much reconstructed cortex must be included before any cluster touches the resection, rather than only checking the single peak vertex. Here wCSET's advantage was unambiguous: it required significantly less cortex than every other method, including Beltrami, to reach the resection — consistent with epilepsy's now well-established character as a network rather than single-generator phenomenon [@spencer_neural_2002; @kramer_epilepsy_2012], in which several regions can jointly sustain a discharge, so that the point of maximal reconstructed activity need not coincide with the tissue whose removal relieves symptoms.

## Epilepsy with Intracranial Electrodes

Against real intracranial recordings, results were more mixed. Of the two subjects with a scalp-visible spike, wCSET significantly outperformed sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE, and CSET in one; in the other, its only advantage was a modest temporal edge over CSET. (The remaining two subjects had deep sources invisible on scalp EEG, where no method reconstructed the intracranial signal well — consistent with this framework's reliance on a fixed-orientation, cortically-constrained source model, which cannot properly represent deeper generators; extending it would require encoding source orientation within the connectivity structure itself, which we leave for future work.) Against Beltrami, however, wCSET was significantly outperformed on at least one metric in both subjects — to our knowledge the first evidence from real, non-simulated activity that a purely geometric account of source reconstruction can match or exceed a connectome-informed one.

## Geometry versus Connectivity

Across all three studies, the Beltrami/GBF geometry-only alternative tracked wCSET more closely than any other competitor, and repeatedly matched or surpassed it: as a surrogate connectome in simulation, as a full method in the resection cohort (though still needing more cortex than wCSET to reach the resection), and against real intracranial recordings in both evaluable subjects. Rather than undermining the case for connectivity-informed reconstruction, this sharpens an open question that earlier, localization-only validations had no way to even pose: whether accurate distributed reconstruction depends on a subject's own long-range white-matter connections, or simply on the coarse, low-frequency structure that geometry and connectomics largely agree on.

## Limitations

Beyond those noted above, our simulation idealizes several aspects of real recordings — known conductivities, a single representative subject, and propagation and noise models that, while physiologically motivated, remain simplified. Clinically, the resection cohort offers only a coarse proxy for the true epileptogenic zone rather than a precise delineation, and the intracranial cohort's evaluable sample — two subjects with a scalp-visible spike — precludes any statistical test across independent subjects, even after correcting each subject's own effective sample size for autocorrelation across channels and timepoints.

# Conclusion

Source reconstruction methods are conventionally benchmarked on their ability to localize a single, focal generator — a criterion that says little about whether a method also captures the distributed, network-level dynamics that connectivity-informed approaches are designed to recover. We introduced wCSET, replacing CSET's L1 sparsity prior with a smooth, exponentially decaying L2 prior over the connectome-harmonic spectrum, and evaluated it — together with CSET, three connectivity-agnostic methods, and a geometry-based (Laplace-Beltrami) alternative — against three independent ground truths for network-level activity: simulated connectome propagation, a resected epileptogenic zone, and simultaneous intracranial recordings.

Across all three, wCSET matched or exceeded standard methods at localizing a source's focal onset, but reconstructed its subsequent spread substantially better: outperforming every connectivity-agnostic competitor and edging out CSET in simulation, requiring markedly less reconstructed cortex to reach the resected zone clinically, and outperforming standard methods and CSET in one of two evaluable intracranial subjects. This advantage was robust to sensor noise, to substantial connectome degradation — wCSET's edge over connectome-agnostic sLORETA never reversed, even under full connectome permutation, unlike CSET's — and to replacing the true connectome with simple, dMRI-free surrogates, indicating the gain rests on coarse, large-scale structure rather than precise individual tractography.

The clearest limit came from the geometry-based Beltrami alternative, which tracked wCSET's performance across all three studies and eventually overtook it. Rather than undercutting the case for connectivity-informed reconstruction, this sharpens an open question earlier, localization-only validations had no way to even pose: whether accurate distributed reconstruction depends on a subject's own white-matter connections, or simply on the coarse structure geometry and connectomics largely agree on.

Beyond wCSET itself, we see the three-part validation framework introduced here — simulated, resected, and intracranial ground truths jointly probing a source's full activity pattern rather than its peak alone — as this work's more durable contribution. Extending it to future connectivity- and geometry-informed methods, and to source models representing deep and multi-generator activity, are natural next steps toward source imaging that reflects the brain's network organization instead of collapsing it back to a single point.

## Synthetic Data — Additional Simulation Details

This section provides implementation-level detail for the synthetic data described in Section 2.1.1.

**Probe-set sampling.** The noise-robustness analysis (Section 3.1.2) sweeps multiple SNR levels per region; doing so across the full 100-region probe set used elsewhere would have been computationally impractical, so a separate, independently-sampled subset of 50 regions was used there instead.

**Propagation model rationale.** A neural mass model [@jansen_electroencephalogram_1995] would capture propagation more physiologically, but such models become unstable at high mass counts, since network size and coupling strength jointly determine dynamical stability [@sanz-leon_mathematical_2015] — which is why other source-reconstruction studies typically cap the number of masses around 1,000, with dipoles spaced roughly 1 cm apart [@siu_structural_2026], a spacing at which the forward model's own point-dipole assumption starts to break down [@nunez_multi-scale_2019]. Our patch-seeded, connectome-driven propagation model avoids this trade-off, keeping the dipole model at high resolution (~7,600 dipoles, ~3.3 mm spacing) while remaining simple enough to generate realistic EEG spikes; we do not claim it is more faithful to reality than neural mass or field models, only that it offers insight a simple patch simulation cannot while staying tractable at high dipole counts.

**Spike waveform.** The spike waveform is a double Hanning window defined as:

$$
s_0(t) = \begin{cases} h\!\left(t,\, \tfrac{2}{3}W\right) & 0 \leq t \leq \tfrac{2}{3}W \\[4pt] -\tfrac{1}{2}\,h\!\left(t - \tfrac{2}{3}W,\; \tfrac{1}{3}W\right) & \tfrac{2}{3}W < t \leq W \end{cases}
$$

where $h(t, T) = \frac{1}{2}\!\left[1 - \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi t}{T}\right)\right]$ is a Hanning window of duration $T$, and $W = 0.05$ s (50 ms) is the total spike duration, chosen to fall centrally within the consensus clinical EEG duration convention for interictal spikes specifically (20–70 ms) [@kane_revised_2017]. The waveform consists of a dominant positive lobe spanning two-thirds of the spike duration, followed by a half-amplitude negative rebound over the remaining third.

**Propagation delay model.** The total propagation delay $\tau_j$ to dipole $j$ was computed as the sum of per-edge delays along the shortest path from the source:

$$
\tau_j = \sum_{(u,v)\,\in\,\mathcal{P}_j} \!\left(\frac{l_{uv}}{v(l_{uv})} + \tau_p\right) + \epsilon_\tau, \qquad v(l) = \begin{cases} 4.5 \text{ mm/ms} & l > 35 \text{ mm (long-range)} \\ 2.5 \text{ mm/ms} & l \leq 35 \text{ mm (U-fiber)} \end{cases}
$$

where $l_{uv}$ is the fiber length of edge $(u,v)$ in mm, and $v(l_{uv})$ is a conduction speed that depends on fiber length: 4.5 mm/ms for long-range tracts above 35 mm — the central estimate of two independent large-sample cortico-cortical evoked potential (CCEP) studies converging on ~3–6 m/s for adult long-range association fibers [@lemarechal_brain_2022; @van_blooijs_developmental_2023] — and a slower 2.5 mm/ms for short-range U-fibers at or below 35 mm, reflecting their distinctly slower reported conduction (~2–3 m/s) relative to long-range tracts [@van_blooijs_developmental_2023]. $\tau_p = 7$ ms is a fixed nodal delay per hop representing synaptic transmission plus relay latency, consistent with the population-level excitatory/inhibitory synaptic time constants (5.8–7.3 ms) estimated directly from CCEP modelling [@lemarechal_brain_2022]. $\epsilon_\tau \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\tau)$, with $\sigma_\tau = 1$ ms, is a per-dipole jitter term modelling uncertainty in propagation timing, accumulated once per hop along the shortest path (i.e. scaling with $\sqrt{h_j}$ rather than a single flat perturbation of the total path delay).

**Noise model derivation.** Sensor-level noise comprised a small fixed instrument/electrode-noise floor (2.0 µV RMS) plus a source-space contribution solved to bring the total delivered sensor-level baseline noise to a target of 15.0 µV RMS — the literature midpoint of the commonly-cited ~10–20 µV RMS scalp EEG background noise range [@nunez_electric_2006]. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was calibrated to a fixed single-trial target of 5 (peak amplitude relative to baseline standard deviation) by scaling the source activity prior to sensor projection: this sits above the ~2.0–3.2 linear-ratio range reported for single-trial interictal spikes [@gonsisko_electroencephalographic_2024], chosen as a practical compromise to keep delivered spikes comfortably above the simulator's own noise floor while remaining much closer to the single-trial literature range than a post-averaging-scale target would be.

**Power analysis.** The number of regions (100) and repetitions (8) per region were set via a power analysis targeting adequate power for the region-paired method comparisons reported throughout the Results, ensuring that the relative ranking of reconstruction methods is robust across a spatially-diverse sample of source regions rather than reflecting any single one; the main effect of method alone was already saturated at power ≈ 1.0 across every tested design.

## Source Reconstruction Framework — Additional Details

**Standard inverse solutions — full derivation.** This section provides the full derivation of the standard inverse solutions (wMNE, dSPM, sLORETA) introduced in Section 2.4.

From a Bayesian perspective, $\mathbf s$ is treated as a random variable with a prior distribution $P(\mathbf s)$ [@knosche_eegmeg_2022]. Assuming a Gaussian prior $\mathbf s \sim \mathcal N(0, \Sigma_{\mathbf s})$, reconstruction becomes a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation, leading to the optimization problem given in Eq. (1) of the main text. There, $\mathbf C$ acts as a weighting matrix derived from the prior covariance, such that $\mathbf C^T\mathbf C = \mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s}^{-1}$. In practice, the true source covariance $\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$ is unknown and replaced with the identity matrix — the assumption of independent, equal-variance sources that gives wMNE, dSPM and sLORETA their "independent-source" label throughout this work.

wMNE additionally adjusts source variances, generating the depth-weighting matrix $\mathbf W_d$ applied to counteract the bias of $l_2$-regularized solutions toward superficial dipoles:

$$
\mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s}^{-1} = \mathbf W_d, \qquad \text{where} \quad W_{d,ii} = \lVert \mathbf L_{:i}\rVert^{-\kappa}
$$

For wMNE, the depth-weighting exponent was set to $\kappa=0.8$, the MEG-optimized value reported by @lin_assessing_2006 (who found a higher optimal range, 2.0–5.0, for EEG specifically). sLORETA and dSPM apply an additional post-hoc standardization on top of the minimum-norm estimate, and were run without additional depth weighting, since this noise-normalization step already compensates for depth bias on its own.

**GBF — full formulation.** wCSET (Eq. 3) is reconfigured to approximate GBF via three changes to its own formulation (not Wang et al.'s exact pipeline — mesh resolution and regularization differ): (i) $\mathbf U$ becomes the Laplace-Beltrami eigenbasis of the cortical mesh (Section 2.3.3) rather than the connectome's; (ii) no depth weighting ($\mathbf W_d = \mathbf I$); and (iii) the exponential weights (Eq. 3) become GBF's hard-truncated, log-form weighting, $W_{h,ii} = \sqrt{-\log(\mu_i/\mu_S)}$ for the $S$ lowest-frequency Beltrami eigenmodes and $W_{h,ii}=0$ beyond ($\mu_i$: Laplace-Beltrami eigenvalues).

**GBF cutoff tuning.** Wang et al. tune a scale parameter $\beta$ for their log-form weighting, but our pipeline trace-renormalizes the inverse kernel before the ridge solve (standard practice), which renders $\beta$ a pure rescale with no effect on the reconstruction. Rather than leave this comparator's one nominally free parameter untuned, we instead tuned the parameter that actually shapes the weighting under our normalization, the cutoff $S$: a sweep against simulated ground truth showed $S=150$ roughly halving peak-localization error relative to $S=300$ (6.1 vs. 14.7 mm) while matching or exceeding it on average precision.

## Volume Conduction Model — Additional Implementation Details

**Head-model pipeline.** Brain tissues were segmented into three compartments (inner skull, outer skull, scalp) using the SimNIBS CHARM pipeline (v4.5; @puonti_accurate_2020). Each compartment mask was smoothed via morphological closing and fitted with a deformable grade-5 icosahedral template.

**Skull-conductivity mismatch precedent.** A similar strategy — perturbing skull conductivity between the forward and inverse models to avoid the inverse crime — has been used elsewhere to probe the sensitivity of EEG source analysis to head-model mismatch [@vorwerk_skull_2014].

## Source Space — Additional Implementation Details

**Surface reconstruction and dipole placement.** The cortical surface was reconstructed using FreeSurfer (v7.4.1). Dipoles were placed via an oct6 icosahedral subdivision (after excluding medial-wall and non-cortical vertices) using MNE-Python (v1.9.0; @gramfort_meg_2013).

**Orientation-constraint rationale.** Dipole orientations were fixed normal to the cortical manifold — a constraint widely adopted in distributed source imaging because the dominant contributors to the EEG signal, pyramidal neurons, have net dipole moments oriented normal to the cortical surface [@dale_improved_1993].

## Signal Preprocessing — Additional Details

**Study 2 filtering parameters.** Data-provider preprocessing (per @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025) included bandpass filtering (high-pass: 0.3–1 Hz; low-pass: 30–100 Hz, with filter settings varying across patients due to the longitudinal nature of the dataset), downsampling to 250 Hz, and interpolation of noisy channels from neighbouring electrodes using 3D splines.

**Study 3 channel-comparison window.** The analysis window around each spike was the continuous interval over which the evoked response's global field power (GFP) stayed above 3 standard deviations of the pre-spike baseline.

## Resected Area Segmentation — Additional Details

**RAMPS input sourcing.** RAMPS requires the resection's hemisphere and lobe (temporal, frontal, parietal, occipital, or a combination thereof) as input: the lobe was unambiguous from the clinical record for temporal resections, and was determined by visual comparison of the pre- and post-operative images for extratemporal resections.

## Network Concentration Index — Additional Details

**Cluster-extent procedure.** NCI is computed as follows: (i) cortical vertices are ranked by absolute source activity magnitude, from highest to lowest; (ii) starting from the top of this ranking, vertices are progressively marked "active", growing the active set one rank at a time; (iii) at each step, the currently active vertices are grouped into spatially contiguous clusters (dipoles adjacent on the cortical mesh), discarding any cluster smaller than 600 mm²; (iv) the procedure stops at the first step where a surviving cluster shares at least one vertex with the resected area. NCI is the percentage of total cortical surface area marked active at that point.

**Chance-level calibration.** The chance level was estimated per subject as the mean, over 200 trials, of independently drawn, spatially unstructured (i.i.d. uniform) per-vertex activity, applying the same cluster-extent procedure with the "touches the resection" requirement removed (i.e. the percentage needed for any cluster, anywhere, to reach the 600 mm² floor).

## Statistical Analysis — Additional Details

**Autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size.** For the paired t-test with effective sample size (used for Study 3's channel/timepoint comparisons), the effective sample size is computed as $n_{\text{eff}} = n / (1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{K} \rho_k)$, where $\rho_k$ is the paired-difference series' own lag-$k$ autocorrelation, summed until it falls within the white-noise 95% confidence band ($1.96/\sqrt{n}$), capped at $n/4$ — the standard correction for testing the mean of a serially-correlated series. This down-weights the nominal pair count to reflect the true amount of independent evidence when neighbouring channels or timepoints are correlated.

**Cluster-based permutation testing.** Continuous comparisons (e.g. across SNR or connectome perturbation severity) used a one-sample, sign-flip permutation test on the paired-difference series (MNE-Python's `permutation_cluster_1samp_test`; 3000 permutations), which identifies contiguous clusters of the coordinate where the two methods differ, rather than testing each point independently. The cluster-forming threshold matched the test's own two-tailed α = 0.05 default; each cluster's p-value reflects how extreme its summed test statistic is relative to the permutation null, and effect size (Cohen's dz) is computed from each subject's difference averaged across the cluster's span.
